Root and Branch Petition
rūt and branch pə-tish'ən
n. (the London petition of December 1640 asking the Long Parliament to abolish episcopacy entirely)
Old Norse rot, root; Old French branche, branch; Latin petitio, a request.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Root and Branch Petition was presented to the House of Commons on 11 December 1640, a month after the Long Parliament first met, by Alderman Isaac Pennington and a crowd of London citizens, bearing some fifteen thousand signatures. It asked that the government of the church by archbishops, bishops, deans, and archdeacons, with all its dependencies, roots and branches, be abolished, and it listed twenty-eight grievances against the bishops: the silencing of godly ministers, the suppression of lectures, the Book of Sports, the Laudian altar policy and bowing toward the communion table, the persecution of conscience in the High Commission, the encouragement of Arminian and popish doctrine, and the corruption of the ecclesiastical courts. Parliament debated the petition and a Root and Branch Bill in 1641; the moderates who wished to reform episcopacy rather than end it resisted, and the division between them became one of the lines along which the nation split into civil war. Episcopacy was finally abolished by ordinance in 1646. The phrase came from the prophet, who foretold a day when the proud would be burned up so that “it shall leave them neither root nor branch” (Mal 4:1), and from Christ: “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up” (Mat 15:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines episcopacy as government of the church by bishops, and to eradicate as to pull up by the roots.

expand to see more

EPIS'COPACY, n. Government of the church by bishops; that form of ecclesiastical government in which diocesan bishops are established, as distinct from and superior to priests or presbyters.

ERAD'ICATE, v.t. To pull up the roots, or by the roots; to destroy any thing that grows.

GRIEV'ANCE, n. That which causes grief or uneasiness; that which burdens, oppresses or injures.

Key Scripture

Mat 15:13 — "But he answered and said, Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up."

Mal 4:1 — "For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch."

1Pe 5:3 — "Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock."

Act 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

Modern Corruption

London's demand that the bishops' government be abolished, not merely reformed.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Petition's premise was that diocesan episcopacy is not a plant of the Father's planting, and that a government which had become an instrument of persecution could not be pruned into health. Peter's charge to elders forbids the very thing the grievances described, ruling “as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3), and Paul names the elders themselves the overseers of the flock (Act 20:28).

The honest caveat is that the abolition of episcopacy came by Parliament and war rather than by the church's own assemblies, and that what replaced it was never fully settled before the Restoration undid it. The principle to recover is that reformation of the church's government must be by Scripture and by the church, and that a root-and-branch reform carried by political force is carried away by the next political force.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ekrizoo (G1610), to root up; phuteia (G5451), a plant; Hebrew shoresh (H8328), root.

Greek phuteia (G5451) — a plant, planting; Matthew 15:13.

Greek ekrizoo (G1610) — to root out, pluck up by the roots; Matthew 15:13.

Hebrew shoresh (H8328) — a root; Malachi 4:1.

Hebrew anaph (H6057) — a branch, bough; Malachi 4:1.

Usage

"“shall be rooted up” (Mat 15:13) — the petitioners' text."

"“neither root nor branch” (Mal 4:1) — the source of the phrase."

"“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3) — the charge against the bishops."
